Reference: Jacobsen et al. (2023)

Model Setting

The paper asks how governments should regulate air pollution from passenger vehicles when the textbook instrument is unavailable. A Pigouvian tax on emissions is technologically infeasible, because measuring the pollution of an individual vehicle is imperfect and prohibitively expensive: roadside remote sensing has large measurement error for a single vehicle, scheduled inspections paired with high-stakes incentives invite avoidance, and gasoline taxes are only a weak proxy for air pollution. Most countries instead rely on exhaust standards, which cap the emission rate (grams per mile) of new vehicles. The paper studies whether the US standards are effective, whether they are cost-effective, and which reforms would raise welfare. It has four parts. First, emissions per mile of new US vehicles have fallen by more than 99 percent since regulation began in the 1960s. Second, regressions that exploit differences in standards between California and federal rules and across vehicle classes, model years and pollutants give an elasticity of emission rates with respect to standards of 0.5 to 1.0, so standards caused between half and all of the decline. Third, standards are not cost-effective, because emission rates rise quickly with vehicle age, vehicles older than 10 years emit most of the pollution, and existing registration fees are higher on newer, cleaner vehicles. Fourth, an analytical model and a quantitative model of the vehicle fleet evaluate counterfactual policies.

The analytical model formalizes the Gruenspecht effect (Gruenspecht 1982): a policy that raises the price of new vehicles raises the price of used vehicles, lowers scrap and extends the life of old, dirty vehicles. It also shows that a registration fee that differs between new and used vehicles by the difference in their pollution damages maximizes welfare. In the quantitative model, the benefits of the Tier 2 standards are 10 to 15 times their costs and each year of earlier adoption is worth 20 to 30 billion dollars, while annual registration fees equal to the pollution damages of each vehicle age and type raise welfare by about 322 billion dollars in present value, mainly by inducing scrap of the oldest vehicles. A fee charged only on new vehicles lowers welfare.

Institutional Background

Hydrocarbons (HC) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) from vehicles were found to contribute to smog in 1952, and by 1959 engineers could abate emissions by running exhaust over a catalyst. Federal exhaust standards regulate HC, NOx and carbon monoxide (CO) per mile for light-duty vehicles (cars) and light-duty trucks. They are separate from fuel economy standards, which target gasoline use and therefore carbon dioxide (CO2). The 1965 Motor Vehicle Air Pollution Control Act created the national Tier 0 standards, expanded by the 1970 Clean Air Act Amendments: CO and HC were regulated from model year 1968 and NOx from 1972, and the limits tightened periodically until 1993. Uncontrolled emission rates are 90 grams per mile for CO, 8.2 for HC and 3.4 for NOx. The car standards fell to 3.4, 0.41 and 1.0 by 1981, which in practice required a catalytic converter on every vehicle from the mid-1970s. Tier 1 (required by the 1990 Amendments, phased in from 1994 and binding in 1996) cut CO and HC limits more for trucks than for cars. Tier 2 was phased in over 2004 to 2009 and applied through 2016, with car limits of 3.4, 0.10 and 0.14 from 2007. Tier 3 is phased in from 2017 to 2025. Tier 0 and Tier 1 are maximum standards for every vehicle in a class, and Tier 2 and Tier 3 add fleet-wide mean standards. California may set its own, tighter standards.

All tiers use the same federal test procedure, a 30-minute driving cycle on a dynamometer. The standard applies to the certification level, which is the test result scaled up by a deterioration factor for the useful life of the vehicle (50,000 miles or 5 years up to 150,000 miles or 15 years). Several years after sale, in-use tests can trigger recalls; between 1975 and 2008 about 80 million vehicles, 16 percent of sales, were recalled. Recall risk leads manufacturers to overcomply, and new-vehicle emission rates are about half of the standards. Catalytic converters lose effectiveness with age because of sulfur in gasoline, wear of the precious metals and failure of complementary parts such as oxygen sensors. Engineers and regulators argue that emission rates would not have fallen without regulation, since consumers neither observe nor value a vehicle's air pollution. About 10 percent of US counties run smog check programs for used vehicles, and 28 states have registration fees that vary with vehicle characteristics, especially value.

Data and Trends

New-vehicle emission rates come from the EPA Annual Certification Test Results Report for model years 1972 to 2019 (keyed in from the Federal Register for 1972 to 1978), and from a 1973 study that applied the federal test procedure to about 1,000 vehicles of model years 1957 to 1971. The used-vehicle data contain 65 million test records. The main source is the Colorado smog check, which uses the IM240 test, a 240-second version of the federal test procedure: about 12 million tests in calendar years 1997 to 2014, covering model years 1982 to 2010, with biennial tests from age four. Only the first test of each inspection sequence is used, to limit manipulation. Sensitivity checks use more than 50 million Colorado remote-sensing readings, smaller samples from 11 other states and from other countries, and California in-use tests. The Leontief inverse of the US input-output table combined with plant-level emissions gives the pollution embodied in manufacturing a vehicle, about 600 dollars of damages per new vehicle in 2000. A new database of state and local registration fees, motor vehicle taxes and vehicle property taxes (together called registration fees) is also built.

Between the 1960s and 2020 the mean emission rate of new vehicles fell by 99.4 percent for CO (from 83 to 0.5 grams per mile), 99.7 percent for HC and 99.5 percent for NOx. Emission rates were flat before standards began and fell in the years when standards tightened. CO2 per mile fell by only 55 percent between 1957 and 2017. Used-vehicle emission rates fell by roughly 90 percent between model years 1982 and 2010.

For new vehicles (17,039 observations) it is 0.54 (0.05), lower because manufacturers already overcomplied.

For CO2, which has no control system that deteriorates, it is 0.72 to 0.95, so part of the gap from one reflects measurement error between the two tests.

  • Other outcomes: standards do not change horsepower or fuel economy, and they lead manufacturers to install cleaner engines. Event-study graphs show that emission rates move in the years when standards change.

Stylized Facts on Cost-Effectiveness

Cost-effectiveness requires equal marginal abatement costs across vehicles, but standards bind only on new vehicles and in-use tests stop at 10 to 15 years. Three facts follow. First, for a given model year, air pollution emission rates rise roughly proportionally with age, and both age and odometer matter independently; CO2 rates do not change with age. Second, in the 2014 Colorado cross-section, 70 to 80 percent of air pollution emissions come from vehicles older than 10 years, and vehicles older than 15 years account for 30 to 50 percent of air pollution but only 10 percent of CO2, although older vehicles are driven less. The mean age of US vehicles doubled from 6 years in 1970 to 12 years in 2018. Third, registration fees fall with age while damages rise: the owner of an 18-year-old vehicle pays 40 dollars less per year than the owner of a 4-year-old vehicle, but the older vehicle causes about 700 dollars more in annual air pollution damages. Existing fees therefore implicitly subsidize pollution.

Analytical Model: Setup and Equilibrium

There is a single vehicle type that lasts at most two periods: it is new (nnn) and then used (uuu). A measure-one continuum of risk-neutral consumers each holds one vehicle, so the numbers of new and used vehicles satisfy N+U=1N+U=1N+U=1 and there is no outside good. The value of a used vehicle is normalized to zero. Willingness to pay for a new vehicle is w≥0w\geq0w≥0, with a continuous distribution G(w)G(w)G(w) that has no mass points and is the same in all periods. New vehicles are supplied by competitive constant-returns manufacturers at producer price ψs\psi^sψs, and the consumer price is ψ=ψs+τ\psi=\psi^s+\tauψ=ψs+τ, where τ\tauτ is a tax on new vehicles. A consumer who buys a new vehicle draws a repair cost kkk from a continuous distribution H(k)H(k)H(k) with density h(k)h(k)h(k). In the next period the consumer either pays kkk and resells the vehicle as used at price ppp in a frictionless competitive market, or scraps it at zero value. The vehicle is repaired if p>kp>kp>k, so the survival share is H(p)H(p)H(p) and the scrap rate is 1−H(p)1-H(p)1−H(p). Supply of used vehicles is:

Us=H(p)N=H(p)1+H(p)(4)U^s=H(p)N=\frac{H(p)}{1+H(p)} \tag{4}Us=H(p)N=1+H(p)H(p)​(4)

where the second equality uses N=1−UN=1-UN=1−U. The expected repair cost conditional on repair is the truncated mean:

kˉ=1H(p)×∫−∞pk dH(k)(5)\bar{k}=\frac{1}{H(p)}\times\int_{-\infty}^{p}k\,dH(k) \tag{5}kˉ=H(p)1​×∫−∞p​kdH(k)(5)

The value of a new vehicle is w−ψw-\psiw−ψ plus the expected resale value net of repair costs, H(p)(p−kˉ)H(p)(p-\bar{k})H(p)(p−kˉ). A consumer buys new if and only if:

w−ψ+H(p)(p−kˉ)>−p(6)w-\psi+H(p)\left(p-\bar{k}\right)>-p \tag{6}w−ψ+H(p)(p−kˉ)>−p(6)

so demand for used vehicles is the share of consumers below the threshold:

Ud=G(ψ−p−H(p)(p−kˉ))(7)U^d=G\left(\psi-p-H(p)\left(p-\bar{k}\right)\right) \tag{7}Ud=G(ψ−p−H(p)(p−kˉ))(7)

H(p∗)1+H(p∗)=G(ψ−p∗−H(p∗)(p∗−kˉ))(8)\frac{H(p^*)}{1+H(p^*)}=G\left(\psi-p^*-H(p^*)\left(p^*-\bar{k}\right)\right) \tag{8}1+H(p∗)H(p∗)​=G(ψ−p∗−H(p∗)(p∗−kˉ))(8)

Supply is increasing and demand is decreasing in ppp, so the interior equilibrium is unique.

A new vehicle creates pollution damages Φ\PhiΦ from production and ϕn\phi^nϕn from exhaust, and a used vehicle creates ϕu>ϕn\phi^u>\phi^nϕu>ϕn. The difference in externalities between a new and a used vehicle is:

Δ≡Φ+ϕn−ϕu(9)\Delta\equiv\Phi+\phi^n-\phi^u \tag{9}Δ≡Φ+ϕn−ϕu(9)

Pollution is a pure externality that consumers ignore. There are two policies. An exhaust standard ω\omegaω constrains new-vehicle exhaust, and tighter standards raise manufacturing cost. Registration fees τn\tau_nτn​ and τu\tau_uτu​ on new and used vehicles are rebated lump sum, and without an outside good only their difference matters:

ϕn≤ω,ψs′(ω)≤0,τ≡τn−τu,ψ=ψs(ω)+τ(10)\phi^n\leq\omega,\qquad\psi^{s\prime}(\omega)\leq0,\qquad\tau\equiv\tau_n-\tau_u,\qquad\psi=\psi^s(\omega)+\tau \tag{10}ϕn≤ω,ψs′(ω)≤0,τ≡τn​−τu​,ψ=ψs(ω)+τ(10)

Welfare is private consumer welfare minus repair and production costs minus the externality.

Analytical Model: Propositions

Proposition 1. A policy that increases ψ\psiψ decreases the scrap rate and increases the market share of used vehicles:

The result can be reconstructed by totally differentiating the equilibrium condition, using that the derivative of H(p)(p−kˉ)H(p)(p-\bar{k})H(p)(p−kˉ) with respect to ppp is H(p)H(p)H(p), so that w∗w^*w∗ falls by 1+H(p∗)1+H(p^*)1+H(p∗) per unit of p∗p^*p∗:

and multiplying by −h(p∗)-h(p^*)−h(p∗) gives the expression in the proposition. A higher new-vehicle price shifts demand toward used vehicles and raises p∗p^*p∗; for any repair cost draw, a higher used-vehicle price makes repair more likely. Tighter standards (a lower ω\omegaω) and higher relative fees on new vehicles (a higher τ\tauτ) both raise ψ\psiψ, so both extend vehicle lifetimes. This is the first formal derivation of the Gruenspecht effect. With an outside good (online appendix) the share of used vehicles in the fleet still rises, but the number of used vehicles can rise or fall because the market contracts.

Proposition 2. Welfare in a time period is maximized when τ=Δ\tau=\Deltaτ=Δ. If τ>Δ\tau>\Deltaτ>Δ, moving to τ′\tau'τ′ with τ>τ′≥Δ\tau>\tau'\geq\Deltaτ>τ′≥Δ increases welfare, and if τ<Δ\tau<\Deltaτ<Δ, moving to τ′\tau'τ′ with τ<τ′≤Δ\tau<\tau'\leq\Deltaτ<τ′≤Δ increases welfare. The intuition is that a consumer who internalized pollution would treat the new-vehicle price as ψs+Δ\psi^s+\Deltaψs+Δ, so the fee difference:

τ=(Φ+ϕn)−ϕu(14)\tau=\left(\Phi+\phi^n\right)-\phi^u \tag{14}τ=(Φ+ϕn)−ϕu(14)

decentralizes the first best for a given exhaust standard, and vehicles survive longer than is socially optimal if and only if τ>Δ\tau>\Deltaτ>Δ. Because the model has one margin (the share of new vehicles), fees that differ by age are a perfect substitute for a tax on emissions. In a richer setting miles driven and maintenance would also respond, and fees would not restore the first best. Exhaust standards on new vehicles alone are a second-best instrument: they lower ϕn\phi^nϕn, but by raising ψs\psi^sψs they lower scrap, while the scrap margin is already distorted whenever τ>Δ\tau>\Deltaτ>Δ. Standards and fees are complements, because faster tightening across model years widens the gap between used and new emissions and raises the return to correcting scrap. A scrap subsidy is not modelled separately; in the model it would act through the same margin as a higher relative fee on used vehicles.

A back-of-envelope calculation splits the 2000 fleet into vehicles up to 9 years old (57 percent of the fleet and 65 percent of miles) and vehicles 10 years or older. Including production emissions, the first group causes 486 dollars of damages per vehicle per year and the second 1,364 dollars, 2.8 times as much, so Δ\DeltaΔ is about −878-878−878 dollars per year. The efficient fee structure taxes used vehicles relative to new ones, whereas existing fees do the opposite.

A vehicle is scrapped when its repair cost exceeds its value, which gives the scrap rate and the supply of used vehicles:

ya,t=ba(pa,t)γa,qa,ts=qa−1,t−1×(1−ya,t)(23)y_{a,t}=b_a\left(p_{a,t}\right)^{\gamma_a},\qquad q^s_{a,t}=q_{a-1,t-1}\times\left(1-y_{a,t}\right) \tag{23}ya,t​=ba​(pa,t​)γa​,qa,ts​=qa−1,t−1​×(1−ya,t​)(23)

Anything that raises used-vehicle values, such as a higher new-vehicle price, lowers scrap at every age, which is the Gruenspecht effect of Proposition 1; a fee on old vehicles lowers their rental rate and value and raises scrap. Suppliers buy new vehicles at price p0,tp_{0,t}p0,t​ until profits are zero, so the new-vehicle rental rate equals depreciation adjusted for repair and scrap:

r0,t=p0,t−(1−y1,t)(p1,t−kˉ1,t1+δ)(24)r_{0,t}=p_{0,t}-\left(1-y_{1,t}\right)\left(\frac{p_{1,t}-\bar{k}_{1,t}}{1+\delta}\right) \tag{24}r0,t​=p0,t​−(1−y1,t​)(1+δp1,t​−kˉ1,t​​)(24)

A competitive equilibrium is a sequence of new-vehicle prices, used-vehicle rental rates, new-vehicle emission rates and fuel economies such that the agent maximizes utility, scrap follows the rule above, manufacturers maximize profits subject to both standards, and supply equals demand for each of the vehicle types. Each period is solved in sequence with Broyden's method. Pollution damages are additively separable and are computed outside the equilibrium algorithm:

Ωt=∑c,s,a,mϕc,s,a,m,t vmtc,s,a θ qc,s,a,m,t+∑c,s,mΦc,s,m,tqc,s,0,m,t(25)\Omega_t=\sum_{c,s,a,m}\phi_{c,s,a,m,t}\,vmt_{c,s,a}\,\theta\,q_{c,s,a,m,t}+\sum_{c,s,m}\Phi_{c,s,m,t}q_{c,s,0,m,t} \tag{25}Ωt​=c,s,a,m∑​ϕc,s,a,m,t​vmtc,s,a​θqc,s,a,m,t​+c,s,m∑​Φc,s,m,t​qc,s,0,m,t​(25)

where ϕc,s,a,m,t\phi_{c,s,a,m,t}ϕc,s,a,m,t​ is exhaust emissions per mile, vmtc,s,avmt_{c,s,a}vmtc,s,a​ is vehicle miles traveled, θ\thetaθ is damages per ton of emissions and Φc,s,m,t\Phi_{c,s,m,t}Φc,s,m,t​ is the damage from manufacturing a new vehicle (the paper prints the last quantity as qc,a,0,m,tq_{c,a,0,m,t}qc,a,0,m,t​). Welfare effects are measured by the equivalent variation; social welfare is consumer plus producer surplus minus pollution damages.

Calibration

There are 2 classes (car, truck), 2 sizes (small, large), 19 age categories (ages 0 to 37 in two-year bins) and 7 manufacturers (Ford, General Motors, Chrysler, Toyota, Honda, other Asian, European), so 28 types per age and 532 vehicle types. The model is calibrated to prices and composition of the 2000 US fleet and follows vehicles to 2020, the period of the Tier 2 rollout. Emission rates by age and type come from the Colorado smog check data of test years 2000 to 2014, with miles traveled by age, class and size. The scrap elasticity γa\gamma_aγa​ is taken from Jacobsen and van Benthem (2015) and varies with class and size, and bab_aba​ is chosen to match baseline scrap rates. The abatement cost parameters χ\chiχ and ζc,s\zeta_{c,s}ζc,s​ are fitted to EPA engineering estimates. Damages per ton θ\thetaθ come from the AP3 integrated assessment model (Tschofen, Azevedo and Muller 2019), which combines county emissions, atmospheric transport, concentration-response functions and the value of a statistical life. The numerical values of the scrap elasticity, the nest elasticities, the discount rate and the damages per ton are reported in the online appendix and not in the main text. Annual damages from new vehicles fell by 77 percent during the Tier 2 rollout.

Counterfactual Results

All policies start in 2000, and effects are cumulative over 20 years in billions of 2019 dollars. Changes in standards are implemented through ϕˉc,s,t\bar{\phi}_{c,s,t}ϕˉ​c,s,t​ and changes in fees through τc,s,a,m\tau_{c,s,a,m}τc,s,a,m​, with fee revenue rebated to the agent and the historical path of standards held fixed.

  • Delaying Tier 2: a four-year delay raises market surplus by 8.2 and pollution damages by 115.3, so welfare changes by −107.2-107.2−107.2, about 27 billion dollars per year; cumulative emissions rise by 8.1 percent (CO), 4.6 percent (HC) and 10.3 percent (NOx). An eight-year delay changes welfare by −184.9-184.9−184.9 (surplus 13.3, damages 198.2).

  • Accelerating Tier 2: four years earlier changes surplus by −9.9-9.9−9.9 and damages by −122.8-122.8−122.8, a welfare gain of 112.9; eight years earlier gives 174.5 (surplus −20.7-20.7−20.7, damages −195.2-195.2−195.2). A uniform 10 percent tightening gives 24.7 (surplus −2.3-2.3−2.3, damages −27.0-27.0−27.0).

  • Cost-effectiveness of standards: the ratio of avoided damages to lost surplus is 10 to 15. At a value of a statistical life of 10 million dollars, Tier 2 avoids about 2,700 deaths per year, 35 percent more than the NOx Budget Program (about 2,000).

  • Age-by-type fee equal to annual damages: surplus changes by −170.6-170.6−170.6 and damages by −492.5-492.5−492.5, a welfare gain of 321.9, with revenue of 1,167.5 (about 60 billion dollars per year). Cumulative emissions fall by 42.3 percent (CO), 42.7 percent (HC) and 24.6 percent (NOx). Vehicles older than 20 years face fees above 2,000 dollars per year, more than their resale value; one third of 15-year-old, half of 20-year-old and 90 percent of 25-year-old vehicles are scrapped.

  • Revenue-neutral age-by-type fee: a feebate that taxes dirty and subsidizes clean vehicles changes surplus by −113.9-113.9−113.9 and damages by −343.7-343.7−343.7, a gain of 229.7. It improves composition but does not shrink the fleet.

  • Fee on new vehicles only: a fee equal to lifetime damages (about 4,500 dollars for the average new vehicle) changes surplus by −16.5-16.5−16.5, raises damages by 3.2 and changes welfare by −19.7-19.7−19.7, with revenue of 399.6. New-vehicle purchases fall by more than 25 percent in the first year and more vehicles aged 15 to 30 survive, the Gruenspecht effect.

  • Flat fee: making existing fees identical across ages and types (up to 50 dollars lower for vehicles younger than five years, up to 30 dollars higher for older ones) raises welfare by 17.5 and lowers emissions by about 2 percent. The inefficiency of current fees is thus mostly the failure to price the externality, not the implicit subsidy.

  • Distribution: households with income below 10,000 dollars own vehicles of mean age near 12 years, against 7 years above 80,000 dollars. Damage-based fees are regressive as a share of income, and more so when revenue is returned per vehicle, while fees on new vehicles fall on richer households but do not cut pollution. Pollution reductions may favour low-income communities, so net incidence is ambiguous.

References

  • Jacobsen, Mark R, James M Sallee, Joseph S Shapiro, and Arthur A Van Benthem. 2023. “Regulating untaxable externalities: Are vehicle air pollution standards effective and efficient?.” The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 138(3): 1907–1976.

This is the estimating equation for the Tier 0 standards, run on cell means for model years 1957 to 1971. The outcome ln⁡Epry\ln E_{pry}lnEpry​ is the log of the mean new-vehicle emission rate (grams per mile) of pollutant ppp in region rrr (California or the rest of the country under federal rules) and model year yyy; the regressor ln⁡Spry\ln S_{pry}lnSpry​ is the log of the exhaust standard, set to the uncontrolled emission rate before a pollutant is regulated, so that the log is defined and the standard is non-binding by construction in those years.

Because both sides are in logs, β1\beta_1β1​ is an elasticity: a one percent tighter standard lowers emission rates by β1\beta_1β1​ percent. A value of one means that emissions track the standard one for one, and a value of zero means that standards are irrelevant. The pollutant-by-region effects ηpr\eta_{pr}ηpr​ absorb permanent differences in levels (for example CO is measured in tens of grams and NOx in single grams), and the model year effects λy\lambda_yλy​ absorb anything common to all pollutants and regions in a year, such as general engine technology. With both sets of effects the design is a difference-in-differences:

β1=Δln⁡Etreated−Δln⁡EcontrolΔln⁡Streated−Δln⁡Scontrol\beta_1=\frac{\Delta\ln E_{\text{treated}}-\Delta\ln E_{\text{control}}}{\Delta\ln S_{\text{treated}}-\Delta\ln S_{\text{control}}}β1​=ΔlnStreated​−ΔlnScontrol​ΔlnEtreated​−ΔlnEcontrol​​

where the treated cells are CO and HC in California from 1966 and federally from 1968, and the controls are the same pollutants in the not-yet-regulated region and NOx and CO2, which are unregulated throughout. Identification requires that, absent standards, log emission rates of regulated and unregulated pollutant-region cells would have moved in parallel. The preferred estimate is 0.80; dropping λy\lambda_yλy​ gives a pure time-series estimate of 0.61.

This is the Tier 1 specification, estimated on individual test readings for model years 1982 to 2000. An observation is a reading of pollutant ppp on vehicle iii of class ccc (car or light truck) and model year yyy, observed at age aaa. The regressor ln⁡Spicy\ln S_{picy}lnSpicy​ is the standard that applied to that class and model year, so β2\beta_2β2​ is again the elasticity of emission rates with respect to the standard.

The three sets of fixed effects determine which variation is left. The pollutant-by-class effects μpc\mu_{pc}μpc​ remove permanent truck-car differences, the pollutant-by-model-year effects νpy\nu_{py}νpy​ remove any change common to cars and trucks of a model year (technology, fuel quality), and the pollutant-by-age effects ξpa\xi_{pa}ξpa​ remove the deterioration profile documented in the stylized facts. What remains is the change over model years in the truck-car gap in standards: Tier 1 tightened CO and HC limits more for trucks than for cars, so

β2≈Δy(ln⁡Etruck−ln⁡Ecar)Δy(ln⁡Struck−ln⁡Scar)\beta_2\approx\frac{\Delta_y\left(\ln E_{\text{truck}}-\ln E_{\text{car}}\right)}{\Delta_y\left(\ln S_{\text{truck}}-\ln S_{\text{car}}\right)}β2​≈Δy​(lnStruck​−lnScar​)Δy​(lnEtruck​−lnEcar​)​

The controls XpicyX_{picy}Xpicy​ (odometer, fuel economy standards, smog check standards, gasoline cost per mile, ethanol share, sulfur content) with coefficient vector π\piπ guard against other policies that changed differentially by class. The identifying assumption is parallel trends between trucks and cars; adding truck-specific linear trends is the demanding check, which lowers the estimate from 0.86 to 0.39. Standard errors are clustered by model year and truck type because the standard varies only at that level. The used-vehicle estimate (0.86 to 1.01) exceeds the new-vehicle one (0.54) because new vehicles already overcomplied.

Tier 2 imposes a fleet-average standard, so there is no vehicle-specific standard to put on the right-hand side. The specification asks a different question: does a cleaner certification result when new carry over to the road years later. The outcome ln⁡Epicyu\ln E^u_{picy}lnEpicyu​ is the log smog-check reading of used vehicle iii, and ln⁡Epicyn\ln E^n_{picy}lnEpicyn​ is the log certification level of the matched new-vehicle type (model years 2000 to 2010). The coefficient β3\beta_3β3​ is the elasticity of used-vehicle emissions with respect to new-vehicle emissions, a pass-through or persistence parameter.

The pollutant-by-model-year effects νpy\nu_{py}νpy​ and pollutant-by-age effects ξpa\xi_{pa}ξpa​ mean that β3\beta_3β3​ is identified from differences across vehicle types within a model year and age, with XpicyX_{picy}Xpicy​ (coefficient ζ\zetaζ) controlling for odometer and other policies. Combining it with the earlier estimates gives the effect of a standard on on-road emissions:

dln⁡Eudln⁡S=dln⁡Eudln⁡En×dln⁡Endln⁡S=β3×dln⁡Endln⁡S\frac{d\ln E^u}{d\ln S}=\frac{d\ln E^u}{d\ln E^n}\times\frac{d\ln E^n}{d\ln S}=\beta_3\times\frac{d\ln E^n}{d\ln S}dlnSdlnEu​=dlnEndlnEu​×dlnSdlnEn​=β3​×dlnSdlnEn​

A value β3=1\beta_3=1β3​=1 would mean proportional persistence. The estimate is about 0.50, but two forces push it below one without implying that standards fail: the certification test and the IM240 smog-check test differ, so ln⁡Epicyn\ln E^n_{picy}lnEpicyn​ is a noisy measure of the true new-vehicle rate and classical measurement error attenuates β3\beta_3β3​; and control systems deteriorate with age. The CO2 regressions separate the two: CO2 has no control system that deteriorates, and its coefficient is 0.72 to 0.95, so the shortfall of that number from one is a gauge of the attenuation from measurement differences alone.

A new vehicle bought in one period becomes a used vehicle in the next period only if its owner repairs it, which happens when the repair cost draw is below the resale price, k<pk<pk<p. Since kkk is drawn from HHH independently across vehicles, the surviving share is Pr⁡(k<p)=H(p)\Pr(k<p)=H(p)Pr(k<p)=H(p). In a stationary equilibrium the number of new vehicles NNN is the same in every period, so the used vehicles on the market today are the survivors of last period's NNN new vehicles:

Us=H(p)NU^s=H(p)NUs=H(p)N

Every consumer holds exactly one vehicle and there is no outside good, so N+U=1N+U=1N+U=1. Substituting N=1−UsN=1-U^sN=1−Us:

The corresponding number of new vehicles is N=1/(1+H(p))N=1/(1+H(p))N=1/(1+H(p)). The supply curve slopes up, because

A higher used-vehicle price makes more owners repair. The used share is at most one half (when H(p)=1H(p)=1H(p)=1 and nothing is scrapped), since each used vehicle must have been a new vehicle one period earlier.

The owner repairs if and only if k<pk<pk<p, so the repair cost actually paid is drawn from HHH truncated above at ppp. The truncated density is h(k)/H(p)h(k)/H(p)h(k)/H(p) on k<pk<pk<p, and its mean is

which is the equation. Note that kˉ\bar{k}kˉ is a function of ppp. The object that enters the consumer problem is the product H(p)(p−kˉ)H(p)(p-\bar{k})H(p)(p−kˉ), the expected resale value net of repair cost. Multiplying out,

H(p)(p−kˉ)=pH(p)−∫−∞pk dH(k)=∫−∞p(p−k)dH(k)=E[max⁡(p−k,0)]H(p)\left(p-\bar{k}\right)=pH(p)-\int_{-\infty}^{p}k\,dH(k)=\int_{-\infty}^{p}\left(p-k\right)dH(k)=\mathbb{E}\left[\max\left(p-k,0\right)\right]H(p)(p−kˉ)=pH(p)−∫−∞p​kdH(k)=∫−∞p​(p−k)dH(k)=E[max(p−k,0)]

so it is the value of the option to repair and resell. Its derivative, by the Leibniz rule, is

ddp[H(p)(p−kˉ)]=H(p)+ph(p)−ph(p)=H(p)\frac{d}{dp}\left[H(p)\left(p-\bar{k}\right)\right]=H(p)+ph(p)-ph(p)=H(p)dpd​[H(p)(p−kˉ)]=H(p)+ph(p)−ph(p)=H(p)

The two terms ph(p)ph(p)ph(p) cancel because the marginal vehicle (with k=pk=pk=p) yields zero net value, an envelope result. This derivative is used in the proofs of equations (11), (13) and (14).

Compare the payoffs of the two choices for a consumer with willingness to pay www. Consumers are risk neutral and there is no discounting between the two periods. Buying new gives the benefit www, costs the consumer price ψ\psiψ, and carries the option to repair and resell next period. The resale option is exercised when k<pk<pk<p and then yields p−kp-kp−k; otherwise the vehicle is scrapped at zero value. Its expected value, from equation (5), is

E[max⁡(p−k,0)]=H(p)(p−kˉ)\mathbb{E}\left[\max\left(p-k,0\right)\right]=H(p)\left(p-\bar{k}\right)E[max(p−k,0)]=H(p)(p−kˉ)

so the payoff from buying new is

Vn(w)=w−ψ+H(p)(p−kˉ)V^n(w)=w-\psi+H(p)\left(p-\bar{k}\right)Vn(w)=w−ψ+H(p)(p−kˉ)

A used vehicle has value normalized to zero, costs ppp and has no resale value because a vehicle lasts at most two periods:

Vu=0−p=−pV^u=0-p=-pVu=0−p=−p

The consumer buys new if and only if Vn(w)>VuV^n(w)>V^uVn(w)>Vu, which is the equation. Rearranged, the condition is

w>ψ−p−H(p)(p−kˉ)w>\psi-p-H(p)\left(p-\bar{k}\right)w>ψ−p−H(p)(p−kˉ)

The right-hand side is the net price premium of a new vehicle: the purchase price difference ψ−p\psi-pψ−p minus the expected net resale value that only a new vehicle carries. This defines the externality of putting one more new vehicle on the road in place of a used one. A new vehicle causes damages Φ\PhiΦ when it is manufactured and ϕn\phi^nϕn from its exhaust; the used vehicle it displaces would have caused ϕu\phi^uϕu. If Δ>0\Delta>0Δ>0 a new vehicle pollutes more than a used one once production is counted; if Δ<0\Delta<0Δ<0 the used vehicle is the dirtier choice.

The standard ω\omegaω in equation (10) lowers ϕn\phi^nϕn and so lowers Δ\DeltaΔ.

This line collects the two policy instruments. The exhaust standard ω\omegaω is a cap on new-vehicle exhaust damages, ϕn≤ω\phi^n\leq\omegaϕn≤ω; a lower ω\omegaω is a tighter standard. The display states the upper-level problem; its solution is the standard CES demand system, which the paper relegates to its online appendix. This defines the per-period user cost of holding a vehicle of class ccc, size sss, age aaa and manufacturer mmm; it is the price that enters the CES demand system. All three are in dollars per vehicle per period and enter additively, so a dollar of fee is equivalent to a dollar of rent from the consumer's point of view.

This is the objective of a new-vehicle manufacturer in period ttt. The firm sells four products (two classes by two sizes) and for each chooses the price pc,s,tp_{c,s,t}pc,s,t​, the exhaust emission rate ϕc,s,t\phi_{c,s,t}ϕc,s,t​ and the fuel economy fc,s,tf_{c,s,t}fc,s,t​. The bracket is the per-vehicle margin: price minus baseline production cost Cc,sbC^b_{c,s}Cc,sb​, minus the cost of emission control Cc,s,tϕC^\phi_{c,s,t}Cc,s,tϕ​ from equation (18), minus the cost of fuel economy improvements Cc,s,tfC^f_{c,s,t}Cc,s,tf​. Emissions do not enter demand: consumers do not value clean exhaust, so a firm never abates voluntarily, and both abatement costs are marginal (per vehicle) and not fixed costs. The maximization is subject to the two constraints in equation (19).

Under Bertrand competition the price condition for product (c,s)(c,s)(c,s), ignoring the fuel economy constraint, is

so the firm internalizes substitution among its own products. The baseline of the paper is perfect competition, modelled as the limit in which demand facing a firm is infinitely price-elastic. Dividing the condition by the own-price derivative and letting it grow without bound drives the margin to zero:

pc,s,t=Cc,sb+Cc,s,tϕ(ϕc,s,t)+Cc,s,tf(fc,s,t)+shadow cost of the fuel economy constraintp_{c,s,t}=C^b_{c,s}+C^\phi_{c,s,t}(\phi_{c,s,t})+C^f_{c,s,t}(f_{c,s,t})+\text{shadow cost of the fuel economy constraint}pc,s,t​=Cc,sb​+Cc,s,tϕ​(ϕc,s,t​)+Cc,s,tf​(fc,s,t​)+shadow cost of the fuel economy constraint

The parameter ζc,s\zeta_{c,s}ζc,s​ is a dollar scale that differs by class and size (controlling a large truck costs more). The factor χt\chi^tχt with χ<1\chi<1χ<1 makes any given level of control cheaper as time passes, representing innovation. The residual ξc,s,t\xi_{c,s,t}ξc,s,t​ is what is left after fitting χ\chiχ and ζc,s\zeta_{c,s}ζc,s​ by least squares to the EPA engineering cost estimates for Tier 2 and Tier 3; adding it back makes the function reproduce the EPA costs exactly along the historical path of standards, while the parametric part extrapolates to counterfactual standards. These are the two regulatory constraints on the manufacturer's problem in equation (17). The first is the exhaust standard: the emission rate of each class-size product may not exceed the cap ϕˉc,s,t\bar{\phi}_{c,s,t}ϕˉ​c,s,t​. Since emission control is costly in equation (18) and consumers do not value it, a firm never goes below the cap, and the paper assumes the constraint binds for every manufacturer. The cap is calibrated to observed emission rates and not to the statutory limit, so the observed overcompliance (new vehicles emit about half the legal standard) is built into the baseline and carried into counterfactuals.

The second is the fuel economy (CAFE) standard for each class ccc (car, truck): the sales-weighted harmonic mean of miles per gallon across the two sizes must be at least fˉc,t\bar{f}_{c,t}fˉ​c,t​. The harmonic mean is used because it equals total miles divided by total gallons when all vehicles drive the same distance. Multiplying out, the constraint is linear in quantities:

∑sqc,s,td(1−fˉc,tfc,s,t)≥0\sum_sq^d_{c,s,t}\left(1-\frac{\bar{f}_{c,t}}{f_{c,s,t}}\right)\geq0s∑​qc,s,td​(1−fc,s,t​fˉ​c,t​​)≥0

Fuel economy standards are held at their historical path in all counterfactuals; they are in the model because they shift new-vehicle prices and operating costs.

This generalizes Us=H(p)NU^s=H(p)NUs=H(p)N in equation (4) to many ages. The two parts together transmit policy to the fleet: anything that raises pa,tp_{a,t}pa,t​, such as a higher new-vehicle price that raises used rental rates, lowers ya,ty_{a,t}ya,t​ and enlarges the stock of old vehicles (the Gruenspecht effect of equation (11)), while a registration fee on old vehicles lowers their rental rate in equation (16), lowers pa,tp_{a,t}pa,t​ and raises scrap.

Rental suppliers can buy a new vehicle from manufacturers at price p0,tp_{0,t}p0,t​. A new vehicle earns the rental rate r0,tr_{0,t}r0,t​ in its first period and then has the same continuation value as in the recursion of equation (21) evaluated at a=0a=0a=0: with probability 1−y1,t1-y_{1,t}1−y1,t​ it is repaired at age 1 and is then worth p1,tp_{1,t}p1,t​ net of the expected repair cost kˉ1,t\bar{k}_{1,t}kˉ1,t​, discounted one period. The value of a new vehicle to a supplier is therefore

r0,t+(1−y1,t)(p1,t−kˉ1,t1+δ)r_{0,t}+\left(1-y_{1,t}\right)\left(\frac{p_{1,t}-\bar{k}_{1,t}}{1+\delta}\right)r0,t​+(1−y1,t​)(1+δp1,t​−kˉ1,t​​)

Suppliers are competitive and can buy any number of new vehicles, so in equilibrium the expected profit on a new vehicle is zero: value equals purchase price,

p0,t=r0,t+(1−y1,t)(p1,t−kˉ1,t1+δ)p_{0,t}=r_{0,t}+\left(1-y_{1,t}\right)\left(\frac{p_{1,t}-\bar{k}_{1,t}}{1+\delta}\right)p0,t​=r0,t​+(1−y1,t​)(1+δp1,t​−kˉ1,t​​)

Solving for the rental rate gives the equation:

r0,t=p0,t−(1−y1,t)(p1,t−kˉ1,t1+δ)r_{0,t}=p_{0,t}-\left(1-y_{1,t}\right)\left(\frac{p_{1,t}-\bar{k}_{1,t}}{1+\delta}\right)r0,t​=p0,t​−(1−y1,t​)(1+δp1,t​−kˉ1,t​​)

The new-vehicle rental rate is first-period depreciation: the purchase price minus the discounted expected value of what is left after one period, allowing for scrap and repair. The difference from ages a≥1a\geq1a≥1 is the direction of causality. For used vehicles the rental rate clears the market and determines the value pa,tp_{a,t}pa,t​; for new vehicles the price p0,tp_{0,t}p0,t​ is pinned down by manufacturers' costs in equation (17), and this condition converts it into the rental rate that enters the user cost in equation (16). It is the analogue of the term ψ−H(p)(p−kˉ)\psi-H(p)(p-\bar{k})ψ−H(p)(p−kˉ) in equation (6) of the analytical model, and it carries the Gruenspecht channel: a tighter standard raises p0,tp_{0,t}p0,t​ and hence r0,tr_{0,t}r0,t​, demand shifts to used vehicles, their rental rates and values rise, and scrap falls by equation (23).

This is the accounting definition of pollution damages in period ttt, in dollars. The first sum is exhaust damages over the whole fleet: for each vehicle type, emissions per mile ϕc,s,a,m,t\phi_{c,s,a,m,t}ϕc,s,a,m,t​ times miles traveled per vehicle vmtc,s,avmt_{c,s,a}vmtc,s,a​ gives emissions per vehicle, multiplying by damages per ton θ\thetaθ converts them into dollars (with a unit conversion from grams to tons, and implicitly a sum over pollutants with pollutant-specific θ\thetaθ from the AP3 model), and qc,s,a,m,tq_{c,s,a,m,t}qc,s,a,m,t​ is the number of vehicles of that type. The second sum is manufacturing damages Φc,s,m,t\Phi_{c,s,m,t}Φc,s,m,t​ per new vehicle times the number of new vehicles.

On the index of the last quantity: the paper's footnote prints qc,a,0,m,tq_{c,a,0,m,t}qc,a,0,m,t​, but throughout the paper the index order is class, size, age, manufacturer, period, and a new vehicle has age a=0a=0a=0, so the intended object is qc,s,0,m,tq_{c,s,0,m,t}qc,s,0,m,t​, summed over c,s,mc,s,mc,s,m as the summation sign indicates. The note's version is the correct one and the printed subscript is a typographical error.

The formula is the many-type version of total damages in the analytical model, (Φ+ϕn)N+ϕuU(\Phi+\phi^n)N+\phi^uU(Φ+ϕn)N+ϕuU from equation (9), with age-specific emission rates in place of ϕn\phi^nϕn and ϕu\phi^uϕu. Policy changes Ωt\Omega_tΩt​ in three ways:

dΩt=∑c,s,a,mvmtc,s,a θ(qc,s,a,m,t dϕc,s,a,m,t+ϕc,s,a,m,t dqc,s,a,m,t)+∑c,s,mΦc,s,m,t dqc,s,0,m,td\Omega_t=\sum_{c,s,a,m}vmt_{c,s,a}\,\theta\left(q_{c,s,a,m,t}\,d\phi_{c,s,a,m,t}+\phi_{c,s,a,m,t}\,dq_{c,s,a,m,t}\right)+\sum_{c,s,m}\Phi_{c,s,m,t}\,dq_{c,s,0,m,t}dΩt​=c,s,a,m∑​vmtc,s,a​θ(qc,s,a,m,t​dϕc,s,a,m,t​+ϕc,s,a,m,t​dqc,s,a,m,t​)+c,s,m∑​Φc,s,m,t​dqc,s,0,m,t​

Standards work through the first term (lower emission rates of new and later of used vehicles), fees mainly through the second (fewer old, dirty vehicles after scrap), and both change new-vehicle sales in the third. Miles traveled are exogenous, so there is no intensive margin. Because Ω\OmegaΩ enters utility additively in equation (15), it does not affect choices and is computed after the equilibrium is solved; social welfare is the equivalent variation of private utility minus the change in Ωt\Omega_tΩt​.
